Source: NRCS,{{PLANTS | taxon = Matricaria discoidea | symbol = MADI6 | accessdate = 2008-06-14 }} GRIN{{Cite web |url = http://www.ars-grin.gov/npgs/ |title = Taxon: ''Matricaria discoidea'' DC. |access-date = 2008-06-14 |author = Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN) |author-link = Germplasm Resources Information Network |date = 2005-09-07 |work = Taxonomy for Plants |publisher = [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]], [[Agricultural Research Service|ARS]], National Genetic Resources Program, National Germplasm Resources Laboratory, Beltsville, Maryland |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080422204654/http://www.ars-grin.gov/npgs/ |archive-date = 2008-04-22 }} |}} '''''Matricaria discoidea''''', commonly known as '''pineappleweed''',{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }} '''wild chamomile''', '''disc mayweed''', and '''rayless mayweed''', is an [[annual plant]] native to North America, [[North Asia|northern Asia]], and [[Europe]] where it grows as a common herb of fields, gardens, and roadsides.{{cite web | url = http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/pineapple-mayweed | title = Pineapple Mayweed | work = NatureGate }} It is in the daisy family [[Asteraceae]]. When crushed, the flowers and foliage emit a strong pineapple-like aroma, giving the plant its common name. ==Description== The flowers of ''M. discoidea'', are small, dome-shaped [[pseudanthium|capitula]] that resemble single flower heads but are composed of densely packed yellowish green [[Petal#Corolla|corollas]].{{Citation |last1=Zargar |first1=Shabir A. |title=Naturalization of Pineapple-weed (Matricaria discoidea DC.) in the Indian Trans-Himalayan region of Ladakh |date=2024-05-22 |url=https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-4306097/v1 |access-date=2025-12-06 |doi=10.21203/rs.3.rs-4306097/v1 |last2=Khuroo |first2=Anzar Ahmad |last3=Reshi |first3=Zafar A. |last4=Ganie |first4=Aijaz Hassan}}{{Cite journal |last1=Inceer |first1=Huseyin |last2=Bal |first2=Murat |date=2019 |title=Morphoanatomical study of Matricaria L. (Asteraceae) in Turkey |url=https://doiserbia.nb.rs/Article.aspx?ID=1821-21581902151I |journal=Botanica Serbica |language=en |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=151–159 |doi=10.2298/BOTSERB1902151I |bibcode=2019BoSer..43..151I |issn=1821-2158|doi-access=free }}{{Cite journal |last1=Claßen-Bockhoff |first1=Regine |last2=Baczyński |first2=Jakub |last3=Hanke |first3=Veronika |last4=Henkes |first4=Svenja Sibylla |last5=Ferdinand |first5=Nadine |date=2025-07-09 |title=Are capitula inflorescences? A reassessment based on flower-like meristem identity and ray flower development |journal=Annals of Botany |volume=137 |issue=1 |article-number=mcaf144 |language=en |doi=10.1093/aob/mcaf144 |pmid=40632900 |pmc=12784083 |issn=0305-7364}} Each plant typically carries at least five capitula, and each capitulum measures 5–15 mm across. The capitula lacks ray [[floret]]s, giving the flowers their distinctive button-like appearance. The capitula are typically solitary or arranged in loose clusters, and they are supported by short [[peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]s about 5–10 mm in length. Papery [[bract]]s (small, leaf-like structures) surround the capitulum in three rows, with membranous margins and rounded tips.{{Cite journal |last1=Arriagada |first1=Jorge E. |last2=Miller |first2=Norton G. |date=1997 |title=The Genera of Anthemideae (compositae; Asteraceae) in the Southeastern United States |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41761535 |journal=Harvard Papers in Botany |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=1–46 |jstor=41761535 |issn=1043-4534}} Like other members of the Asteraceae family, it produces florets with an inferior ovary.{{Cite journal |last1=Munro |first1=Marian C. |last2=Newell |first2=Ruth E. |last3=Hill |first3=Nicholas M. |date=2014 |title=3-9 Asteraceae, aster family |url=https://ojs.library.dal.ca/NSM/article/view/5321 |journal=Nova Scotia Museum |language=en}} The hollow, conical receptacle contains numerous tubular, bisexual disc florets, each with five stamens and a [[pistil]] formed from two fused carpels. There are no scales between the disc florets. ''Matricaria'' species have flattened and penicillate style branches, aiding in pollen transfer. Flowerheads are commonly produced from March to September. The leaves are [[Pinnation|pinnately divided]] one to three times, with blades measuring approximately 10–65 mm long and 2–20 mm wide.{{Cite web |last=Huette |first=T |date=September 29, 2025 |title=Invasive Plants and Exotic Weeds of Southeast Alaska |url=https://www.invasive.org/weedcd/pdfs/se_inv_plnt_guide1.pdf |access-date=September 29, 2025 |website=invasive.org}}{{Cite web |title=Matricaria discoidea - FNA |url=https://floranorthamerica.org/Matricaria_discoidea |access-date=2025-12-06 |website=floranorthamerica.org}} As an annual species, the leaves [[Plant senescence|senesce]] along with the rest of the plant at the end of each growing season.[[File:Trichomes on upper surface of Matricaria discoidea leaf.jpg|thumb|Translucent trichomes on the upper surface of a ''Matricaria discoidea'' leaf|alt=Translucent trichomes on the upper surface of a Matricaria discoidea leaf|left]] [[File:Detail on the midvein of a Matricaria discoidea leaf.jpg|thumb|Detail on the midvein of a ''Matricaria discoidea'' leaf|alt=Detail on the midvein of a Matricaria discoidea leaf.|left]]Although the foliage appears glabrous, under high magnification it has many microscopic trichomes made of short basal cells and a long, pointed terminal cell.{{Cite web |last1=Patton |first1=Aaron |last2=Beck |first2=Leslie |last3=Daniel |first3=Kyle |title=Spotlight on Weeds: Pineapple weed |url=https://purduelandscapereport.org/article/spotlight-on-weeds-pineapple-weed/ |access-date=2025-12-06 |website=Purdue Landscape Report |date=24 May 2022 |language=en-US}}{{Cite journal |last1=Inceer |first1=Huseyin |last2=Ozcan |first2=Melahat |date=2011-10-01 |title=Leaf anatomy as an additional taxonomy tool for 18 taxa of Matricaria L. and Tripleurospermum Sch. Bip. (Anthemideae-Asteraceae) in Turkey |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00606-011-0487-2 |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |language=en |volume=296 |issue=3 |pages=205–215 |doi=10.1007/s00606-011-0487-2 |bibcode=2011PSyEv.296..205I |issn=1615-6110|url-access=subscription }} Microscopically, the leaves are amphistomatic, with stomata present on both the adaxial and abaxial surfaces, positioned close to the epidermis and flanked by oval-shaped [[guard cell]]s. The cuticle is thin (~2.6 μm), and the leaf surfaces show little difference between top and bottom. Each square millimeter of the upper leaf surface contains 205 stomata on average, while the lower surface contains an estimated 142 stomata per mm2. Internally, leaves have one large and two medium vascular bundles, along with accessory bundles and secretory canals (resin ducts) distributed throughout the mesophyll. Consistent with most Asteraceae, ''M. discoidea'' uses the {{Chem|C|3}} photosynthetic pathway.{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Hong |last2=Liu |first2=Weiguo |last3=Leng |first3=Qin |last4=Hren |first4=Michael T. |last5=Pagani |first5=Mark |date=2011-03-01 |title=Variation in n-alkane δD values from terrestrial plants at high latitude: Implications for paleoclimate reconstruction |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0146638011000088 |journal=Organic Geochemistry |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=283–288 |doi=10.1016/j.orggeochem.2011.01.006 |bibcode=2011OrGeo..42..283Y |issn=0146-6380|url-access=subscription }} ''M. discoidea'' has a shallow root system defined by a short, thick [[taproot]] with many fine secondary fibrous roots. The taproot descends directly from the seed's embryo and grows vertically downward. ==Distribution and habitat== The plant thrives in disturbed areas, especially those with poor, compacted [[soil]]. It often blooms along footpaths and roadsides in spring and early summer. It occurs across Canada and the United States, especially as a common weed in Alaska, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories.{{Cite book |last=Walsh |first=Stanley L. |title=Anderson's flora of Alaska and adjacent parts of Canada. |publisher=Brigham Young University Press |year=1974 |isbn=0-8425-0705-1 |location=Provo}} However, there is disagreement over whether it originated in North America or in Siberia.{{cite web |title=Matricaria discoidea DC |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:154716-2 |access-date=21 February 2024 |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew}}{{cite web |last1=Brouillet |first1=Luc |date=5 November 2020 |title=''Matricaria discoidea'' - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Matricaria_discoidea |access-date=21 February 2024 |website=Flora of North America}} This species has been introduced to Europe, Asia, Iceland, South America, and New Zealand{{Cite book |last=Hultén |first=Eric |title=Flora of Alaska and Neighboring Territories |date=June 1968 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=9780804706438 |location=Stanford, CA}} and is now widespread and naturalized in Britain, where it has become one of the fastest-spreading plants of the 20th century.{{cite web |editor=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |title=Matricaria discoidea DC |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.5cm |access-date=21 February 2024 |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland}}The Wildlife Trusts, "Pineappleweed" http://www.wildlifetrusts.org/species/pineappleweed == Reproduction == [[File:Aboveground plant body of pineapple weed (Matricaria discoidea).jpg|thumb|Aboveground plant body of ''Matricaria discoidea'']] ''M. discoidea'' reproduces solely through seed formation.Densmore R., McKee P.C., and Roland C. 2001. “Exotic Plants in Alaskan National Park Units.” https://accs.uaa.alaska.edu/wp-content/uploads/Exotic_Plants_in_Alaskan_National_Park_Units.pdf The flower heads produce small, light brown, ribbed seeds measuring 1.3–1.6 mm in length by <0.7 mm in width and weighing 0.14 mg on average.Royer F. and Dickinson R. 1999. ''Weeds of the Northern U.S. and Canada: A Guide for Identification''. University of Alberta. ISBN 978-1-55105-221-2. Google-Books-ID: [https://books.google.com/books?id=ebFUcfN2enIC ebFUcfN2enIC]. Accessed September 20, 2025.{{Cite journal |last=Dostál |first=Petr |date=2010-12-01 |title=Post-dispersal seed mortality of exotic and native species: Effects of fungal pathogens and seed predators |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1439179110001283 |journal=Basic and Applied Ecology |volume=11 |issue=8 |pages=676–684 |doi=10.1016/j.baae.2010.10.001 |bibcode=2010BApEc..11..676D |issn=1439-1791|url-access=subscription |hdl=11104/0195992 |hdl-access=free }} Each seed is enveloped in a 19.6–22.8 μm-thick seed coat and packaged in a small, dry, [[indehiscent]] fruit [[achene]].Shil A. and Mukherjee S. K. 2016. "[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/310476973_DIVERSITY_OF_CYPSELAR_ANATOMY_IN_NINE_SPECIES_OF_THE_TRIBE_ANTHEMIDEAE_ASTERACEAE Diversity of cypselar anatomy in nine species of the tribe Anthemideae (Asteraceae).]" ''Indian Journal of Plant Sciences'', 5(3), 95-105. ISSN: 2319–3824. DOI:10.13140/RG.2.2.16660.50561 Flowering occurs rapidly under favorable conditions. In temperate environments such as England, ''M. discoidea'' may flower only 37–50 days after seedling emergence, depending on temperature and day length.{{Cite journal |last1=Roberts |first1=H. A. |last2=Feast |first2=Patricia M. |date=1974 |title=Observations on the Time of Flowering in Mayweeds |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2402017 |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=223–229 |doi=10.2307/2402017 |jstor=2402017 |bibcode=1974JApEc..11..223R |issn=0021-8901|url-access=subscription }} Shorter [[photoperiod]]s and later-season [[germination]] extend the time to flowering, often causing [[overwintering]] as a rosette before blooming the following spring. Individual flower heads produce 50–400 seeds.ADHB. 2008. "Distribution and biology of pineappleweed in the UK." Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. https://ahdb.org.uk/knowledge-library/distribution-and-biology-of-pineappleweed-in-the-uk The main plant has been observed to produce up to six thousand seeds in the United Kingdom, while in Alaska the main plant usually contains 11–1000 seeds. Pineapple weed readily fertilizes itself,{{Cite journal |last1=Mitsuoka |first1=Sachihiko |last2=Ehrendorier |first2=Friedrich |date=1972-02-01 |title=Cytogenetics and evolution of Matricaria and related genera (Asteraceae-Anthemideae) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01373265 |journal=Österreichische botanische Zeitschrift |language=en |volume=120 |issue=1 |pages=155–200 |doi=10.1007/BF01373265 |bibcode=1972PSyEv.120..155M |issn=1615-6110|url-access=subscription }}{{Cite journal |last=Ehrendorfer |first=Friedrich |date=1970 |title=Evolutionary Patterns and Strategies in Seed Plants |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2307/1217953 |journal=Taxon |language=en |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=185–195 |doi=10.2307/1217953 |jstor=1217953 |bibcode=1970Taxon..19..185E |issn=1996-8175|url-access=subscription }} and the species typically produces seeds one or more times per year. Buried ''M. discoidea'' seeds have been found to quickly lose viability at an estimated rate of 15% per year over their first ten years, although they generally remain viable for a minimum of three years.Conn J. S., Beattie K. L., and Blanchard A. 2006. "Seed Viability and Dormancy of 17 Weed Species after 19.7 Years of Burial in Alaska." Weed Science, 54(3), 464-470. https://doi.org/10.1614/WS-05-161R.1 Similarly, seeds experience a steep decline in [[dormancy]] in the initial years after burial. Successful germination requires light and open, disturbed soil, as seeds buried too deeply will not sprout. == Ecology == Seeds are very easily dispersed by water, adhesion to animals, human activity, and motor vehicles. A study by Dunmail J. Hodkinson and Ken Thompson found that ''M. discoidea'' is one of the most common plants to be transported in this way.{{Cite journal |last1=Hodkinson |first1=Dunmail J. |last2=Thompson |first2=Ken |date=1997 |title=Plant Dispersal: The Role of Man |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2405264 |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=34 |issue=6 |pages=1484–1496 |doi=10.2307/2405264 |jstor=2405264 |bibcode=1997JApEc..34.1484H |issn=0021-8901|url-access=subscription }} The roots of pineapple weed are colonized by [[Arbuscular mycorrhiza|arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi]].{{Cite book |last=Štajerová, Marie Šmilauerová, Šmilauer |first=K., M., P. |title=Arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis of herbaceous invasive neophytes in the Czech Republic |date=2009 |pages=Preslia 81, 341–355}}{{Cite journal |last1=Sokornova |first1=Sonya |last2=Malygin |first2=Daniil |last3=Terentev |first3=Anton |last4=Dolzhenko |first4=Viktor |date=2022-12-18 |title=Arbuscular Mycorrhiza Symbiosis as a Factor of Asteraceae Species Invasion |journal=Agronomy |language=en |volume=12 |issue=12 |pages=3214 |doi=10.3390/agronomy12123214 |bibcode=2022Agron..12.3214S |doi-access=free |issn=2073-4395}} These mycorrhizae give the plant greater access to water as well as nutrients like phosphorus, nitrogen, sulfur, and trace elements. Despite ''M. discoidea''{{'}}s ability to self-pollinate, insect pollination also occurs.{{Cite journal |last1=Géron |first1=Charly |last2=Lembrechts |first2=Jonas J. |last3=Hamdi |first3=Rafiq |last4=Berckmans |first4=Julie |last5=Nijs |first5=Ivan |last6=Monty |first6=Arnaud |date=2022-12-01 |title=Phenotypic variation along urban-to-rural gradients: an attempt to disentangle the mechanisms at play using the alien species Matricaria discoidea (Asteraceae) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11258-022-01269-y |journal=Plant Ecology |language=en |volume=223 |issue=10 |pages=1219–1231 |doi=10.1007/s11258-022-01269-y |bibcode=2022PlEco.223.1219G |issn=1573-5052}}{{Cite journal |last1=Gresty |first1=Catherine E. A. |last2=Clare |first2=Elizabeth |last3=Devey |first3=Dion S. |last4=Cowan |first4=Robyn S. |last5=Csiba |first5=Laszlo |last6=Malakasi |first6=Panagiota |last7=Lewis |first7=Owen T. |last8=Willis |first8=Katherine J. |date=2018 |title=Flower preferences and pollen transport networks for cavity-nesting solitary bees: Implications for the design of agri-environment schemes |journal=Ecology and Evolution |language=en |volume=8 |issue=15 |pages=7574–7587 |doi=10.1002/ece3.4234 |doi-access=free |issn=2045-7758 |pmc=6106195 |pmid=30151172 |bibcode=2018EcoEv...8.7574G }} Its pollen has been identified in brood cells of ''[[Megachile versicolor]]'' (leafcutter bee). [[Meadow brown|Butterflies]] have also been known to drink nectar from the flowers of ''Matricaria'' species.{{Cite journal |last=Dover |first=John W. |date=1996 |title=Factors Affecting the Distribution of Satyrid Butterflies on Arable Farmland |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2404943 |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=33 |issue=4 |pages=723–734 |doi=10.2307/2404943 |jstor=2404943 |bibcode=1996JApEc..33..723D |issn=0021-8901|url-access=subscription }} == Uses == The greens can be washed and eaten, and both the flowers and the whole plant can be steeped to make tea,{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}} described as "excellent" by one field guide.{{Cite book|last=Benoliel|first=Doug|title=Northwest Foraging: The Classic Guide to Edible Plants of the Pacific Northwest|publisher=Skipstone|year=2011|isbn=978-1-59485-366-1|edition=Rev. and updated|location=Seattle, WA|pages=123|oclc=668195076}} They have also been used in salads (although they may become bitter by the time the plant blooms). Extracts from the flowers and other aerial parts of the plant have been shown to possess non-toxic, pain-relieving, and mildly sedative effects, reflecting the biological activity concentrated in the floral tissues.{{Cite journal |last1=Sepp |first1=Janne |last2=Koshovyi |first2=Oleh |last3=Jakštas |first3=Valdas |last4=Žvikas |first4=Vaidotas |last5=Botsula |first5=Iryna |last6=Kireyev |first6=Igor |last7=Severina |first7=Hanna |last8=Kukhtenko |first8=Oleksandr |last9=Põhako-Palu |first9=Kaisa |last10=Kogermann |first10=Karin |last11=Heinämäki |first11=Jyrki |last12=Raal |first12=Ain |date=2024-03-18 |title=Phytochemical, Pharmacological, and Molecular Docking Study of Dry Extracts of Matricaria discoidea DC. with Analgesic and Soporific Activities |journal=Biomolecules |language=en |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=361 |doi=10.3390/biom14030361 |doi-access=free |issn=2218-273X |pmc=10968509 |pmid=38540779}} ==Gallery== File:Matricaria discoidea 2637.JPG|The [[pinnate]]ly dissected leaves are sweet-scented when crushed.
